title: Rivers of air
hook: Ten kilometres up, winds of 200 km/h circle the planet. Planes ride them east.
notes: Winds at the 250 hPa pressure level (about 10 km up) from the NOAA/NCEP Global Forecast System analysis of 13 October 2026, 12:00 UTC, on a 1° grid. One moment in time: the jet streams shift and wander from day to day. Flight times are typical scheduled times and vary by airline and season.

scenes.title: Winds at airliner height
scenes.text: Each streak is a parcel of air drifting with the wind at about the height where airliners cruise. Bright streaks move faster than 35 metres per second, about 125 km/h. Two wavy bands stand out over the mid-latitudes: the jet streams.

scenes.title: Faster going east
scenes.text: The jet streams blow from west to east. A flight from New York to London rides the tailwind and is usually about an hour shorter than the same flight going the other way.

scenes.title: The southern jet
scenes.text: The southern hemisphere has its own jet stream, circling Antarctica over open ocean. With few mountains to disturb it, it is often steadier than the northern one.

scenes.title: Weather makers
scenes.text: The jet streams steer storms and separate cold polar air from warmer air to the south. When they buckle into big loops, cold or hot spells can stall over a region for days.
